timeline.student: Hello, I am a medical student. I will listen to your concerns, examine you with your permission, and discuss the next steps.
timeline.patient: Hello. Thank you for introducing yourself. I am ready to talk.

timeline.student: What brings you in today?
timeline.patient: My left calf cramps whenever I walk a couple of blocks.
timeline.why: Distinguish vascular walking pain from posture-dependent or muscular pain.

timeline.student: When did the calf pain start?
timeline.patient: It started about 3 months ago.
timeline.why: Does standing still relieve it, or must you sit and bend forward?

timeline.student: How has your walking distance changed?
timeline.patient: At first I could walk six blocks. Now it starts after about two.
timeline.why: Change over time can change urgency even when the symptom is familiar.

timeline.student: Where is the pain?
timeline.patient: It is in the back of my left calf.

timeline.student: Does the calf pain spread?
timeline.patient: It stays in the calf.
timeline.why: Spread of discomfort can connect an apparent local complaint with another system.

timeline.student: What does the calf pain feel like?
timeline.patient: A tight cramp, as if the muscle is squeezing.
timeline.why: Use the patient’s words before translating them into a clinical description.

timeline.student: How severe is the calf pain?
timeline.patient: About 6 out of 10. I have to stop walking.
timeline.why: Intensity and functional effect are distinct; record only the dimension answered.

timeline.student: How long does each cramp last?
timeline.patient: It settles within about 3 minutes after I stop.
timeline.why: Separate time since onset from duration of one episode and from continuity.

timeline.student: What activity brings on the calf pain?
timeline.patient: Walking fast or uphill brings it on sooner.

timeline.student: Do you have to sit or bend forward to relieve it?
timeline.patient: No. Just standing still is enough.
timeline.why: Relief changes probability, but is not proof that a serious cause is excluded.

timeline.student: Does standing still bring on pain?
timeline.patient: No, standing still does not cause it.
timeline.why: Compare triggers with the chronology; one trigger does not establish a diagnosis.

timeline.student: What have you tried for the calf pain?
timeline.patient: I tried stretching, but it did not help.

timeline.student: Have you had this before these three months?
timeline.patient: No, this is new for me.

timeline.student: Have you had back pain?
timeline.patient: My lower back sometimes aches after a long shift, but it does not spread down my leg.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Have you had myalgia?
timeline.patient: Only that left calf cramps with walking.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Do you have foot pain at rest or sores that will not heal?
timeline.patient: No pain at rest and no sores.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you had chest pain?
timeline.patient: I have not had chest pain.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you had dyspnea?
timeline.patient: I am not short of breath.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you had edema?
timeline.patient: Neither leg has been swollen.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Any other joint pain?
timeline.patient: My hip and knee do not hurt.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you had numbness?
timeline.patient: My feet do not feel numb.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you had tingling?
timeline.patient: I have not had pins and needles.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you noticed weakness?
timeline.patient: My leg is not weak; I stop because of the cramp.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: What medical conditions do you have?
timeline.patient: I have high blood pressure and high cholesterol.

timeline.student: Have you been diagnosed with diabetes?
timeline.patient: No, I have not been diagnosed with diabetes.

timeline.student: What operations have you had?
timeline.patient: My appendix was removed when I was 19.

timeline.student: What medicines do you take?
timeline.patient: Lisinopril 20 milligrams every morning. I stopped atorvastatin 20 milligrams 6 months ago because the refill was expensive.
timeline.why: Name, dose and frequency matter; do not fill in missing details.

timeline.student: Do you have medication allergies?

timeline.why: Distinguish the substance and reaction from a blanket allergy label.

timeline.student: Do you smoke?

timeline.student: How much alcohol do you drink?
timeline.patient: One beer on most Saturday evenings.

timeline.student: Do you use recreational drugs?
timeline.patient: No.

timeline.student: What do you do for work?
timeline.patient: I supervise a warehouse. Walking the floor has become difficult.

timeline.student: Who lives with you?
timeline.patient: My husband lives with me and can drive me to appointments.

timeline.student: What health problems did your father have?
timeline.patient: My father had a heart attack at 54.
timeline.why: Record which relative and the condition; do not infer a family history from patient worry.

timeline.student: What health problems does your mother have?
timeline.patient: My mother has type 2 diabetes.

timeline.student: Do you have siblings and are they healthy?

note.S:
CC: My left calf cramps whenever I walk a couple of blocks.

HPI: 59-year-old male. Three months of exertional left calf pain. Pain is localized to the left calf. No radiation. Cramping tightness. 6/10 and limits walking. Resolves within 3 minutes of rest. Walking threshold decreased from six to two blocks. Provoked earlier by brisk walking or hills. Standing rest suffices without lumbar flexion. Not provoked by standing alone. Stretching ineffective. No earlier episodes.

PMH: Hypertension and hyperlipidemia. No known diabetes.

PSH: Appendectomy at 19.

Meds: Lisinopril 20 mg daily; stopped atorvastatin 20 mg 6 months ago because of cost.

SH: Current tobacco: 35 pack-years. Approximately one beer weekly. No recreational drugs. Warehouse supervisor; walking duties limited. Lives with husband; transport available.

FH: Father: myocardial infarction at 54. Mother: type 2 diabetes. Younger sister: hypertension.

Allergies: Penicillin: hives, no respiratory reaction.

ROS: Cardiovascular: No chest pain. No dyspnea. No edema. Musculoskeletal: Occasional nonradiating low-back ache after work. No hip or knee pain. Exertional left calf cramping. Neurologic: No numbness. No paresthesias. No focal weakness. No rest pain or nonhealing wounds.
note.O:
Vitals: BP 148/86 mmHg, P 78 bpm, R 16 rpm, T 98.4 F oral, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5' 10", Wt 194 lbs

General: Alert, comfortable at rest, without respiratory distress.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm without murmur.
Lungs: Breath sounds clear bilaterally.
Heart: Left dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses 1+; right pedal pulses 2+.
Extremities: Left foot slightly cooler than right; capillary refill 3 seconds left and 2 seconds right. No edema or calf asymmetry.
Skin: Reduced hair over the left lower leg; no ulcer or tissue loss on inspected legs and feet.
Musculoskeletal: No focal calf or knee tenderness. Mild bilateral lumbar paraspinal tenderness.
Neurologic: Light touch intact in both feet.
Musculoskeletal: Ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion 5/5 bilaterally.
Osteopathic: L3 bilateral lumbar paraspinal tissue texture change and tenderness.
A: 1. Peripheral artery disease with intermittent claudication
2. Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
P: 1. Obtain resting ankle-brachial indices and assess cardiovascular risk; use exercise ABI if resting results are nondiagnostic. If PAD is confirmed, discuss single antiplatelet and high-intensity statin therapy after contraindication review, structured walking, smoking cessation and daily foot care. Address refill cost; review in 2 weeks. Sudden persistent pain, pallor, coldness or weakness needs emergency care.

2. If vascular testing does not explain symptoms, reassess posture dependence and neurologic findings; pursue lumbar evaluation as indicated. Encourage tolerable activity and explain emergency bladder, saddle-sensation or weakness symptoms.

3. If a muscular cause remains likely after vascular assessment, use relative rest, gentle rehabilitation and safe analgesia rather than forcing painful exercise. Explain a gradual return to work and activity after vascular causes have been assessed.

walkthroughs.estimate_method: 150 spoken words/minute plus the full simulation examination durations and 55 seconds for introductions and transitions; explanatory commentary excluded. This is a planning estimate, not a measured student performance.

reasoning.question: Does standing still relieve it, or must you sit and bend forward?
reasoning.why: Distinguish vascular walking pain from posture-dependent or muscular pain.
reasoning.if_present: Use the reported pattern to select the relevant examinations and assess urgency.
reasoning.if_absent: Keep alternatives open and ask a focused follow-up.
reasoning.document: Separate reported symptoms, observed signs, assessment and proposed care.

differentials.name: Peripheral artery disease with intermittent claudication
aliases: Peripheral artery disease with intermittent claudication
differentials.teaching_context: Reproducible exertional calf pain, rapid standing-rest relief and asymmetric pedal pulses support arterial disease.

differentials.name: Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
aliases: Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
differentials.teaching_context: Exertional leg symptoms and back discomfort warrant consideration; lack of posture dependence and pulse asymmetry argue against it as the main cause.

differentials.name: Calf muscle overuse or strain
differentials.teaching_context: Walking-related muscular pain is possible, but progression and vascular findings favor arterial disease.

omissions: Explaining uncertainty and the practical follow-up plan.
